endorsements.quote: Before deploying any AI that will use patient data or interact with the patient, obtain informed consent and document this in the record.
For instance, if consultations will be recorded for an AI scribe, the patient must agree to that recording, knowing who will have access to the audio or transcript.
Educating patients about the tool’s purpose and limitations is also critical to set appropriate expectations.
If an AI is summarising session notes, the GP needs to review those summaries for accuracy to ensure no critical information is lost or misinterpreted.
Accordingly, AI should be regarded as a decision-support tool rather than a replacement for clinical judgement, with diagnostic and treatment decisions always requiring human oversight.
Clinicians should be ready to override or disregard AI advice if it contradicts their clinical judgment or patient preferences.
It is also important to avoid over- reliance on AI.

Such training should go beyond basic technical literacy to include understanding of data ethics, algorithmic bias, medico-legal accountability and the appropriate use of AI in sensitive areas such as mental health.
This is especially vital in high-risk situations, such as acute suicidality or manic episodes, where AI should only assist, not act autonomously.

Future research should include rigorous clinical trials and real-world implementation studies in general practice, testing AI-assisted interventions – for example, comparing outcomes from GP + AI care versus standard GP care alone.
Educating patients about the tool’s purpose and limitations is also critical to set appropriate expectations.
Patients should understand what the tool does, what data it collects and any privacy implications.

unlisted_practices: Introduce AI mental health tools first with stable patients with mild-to-moderate symptoms rather than those in crisis or with complex psychiatric conditions.
Introduce AI tools as one component of a comprehensive care plan, not a standalone solution, and incorporate check-ins about the tool into follow-up appointments.
Use purpose-built, evidence-based digital mental health tools with embedded safeguards that restrict unsafe outputs and align responses with clinical guidelines.
Guide patients toward digital mental health platforms that meet robust privacy and security standards.
Employ digital navigators to help people with low digital health literacy use AI-enabled mental health services.
Establish GP digital champions or designated technology leads within practices to curate trusted tools and guide safe integration.
Integrate AI education into undergraduate medical curricula and ongoing professional development for GPs.
Ensure AI tools interoperate with existing EMR platforms to avoid manual data transfer and duplicate record keeping.
Develop sustainable reimbursement frameworks and clear billing guidance for AI-assisted consultations to avoid widening inequities.
